[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] CyrusOne was founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten, who had previously built companies acquired by IXC Communications. The company was purchased by Cincinnati Bell for 525 million dollars in 2010, completed an IPO in 2013, and was taken private again in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts and Global Infrastructure Partners acquired it for 15 billion dollars. Sourcing fetched this session gave detailed acquisition stories for several CyrusOne markets, including Texas, Virginia, Ohio, Arizona, Illinois, and Connecticut, but did not contain a specific opening date, investment figure, or building history for this particular state cluster. reading.body:
CyrusOne's Durham campus publishes 40 MW of IT capacity across 420,000 square feet, enough to support roughly 1,000 GPU training racks or 4,000 colocation racks depending on density.

The 95 watts per square foot of technical space at full load indicates moderate density, consistent with mixed-use colocation rather than purpose-built high-density AI infrastructure. This matters because AI training workloads, which now drive marginal demand for data center power, typically require higher power density and specialized cooling and power delivery. CyrusOne's published specs do not disclose redundancy architecture, cooling technology, or fiber connectivity, so the facility's suitability for cutting-edge AI workloads cannot be assessed from available data.

Within North Carolina, this campus ranks first by disclosed IT capacity. However, 19 facilities are mapped in the state and only this one has published a megawatt figure. That ranking reflects sparse disclosure rather than actual market dominance. The absence of published specifications from 18 other North Carolina facilities means the state's true installed capacity, and its role in the national power budget for AI compute, remains opaque.
